 Social Security's 'Trump Bump' COLA Just Hit a Milestone Not Seen Since 1997
 The 2027 COLA marks a historic milestone and brings a welcome benefits bump.
 By
 Paige Cerulli 
 ,
 Edited by
 Laura Hohenstein 
 Updated
 Nov. 3, 2026
 Fact checked 
 This article was subjected to a comprehensive fact-checking process. Our professional fact-checkers verify article information against primary sources, reputable publishers, and experts in the field.
 Add Us On Google
 Google Preferred Sources lets you customize your search results. By choosing to follow FinanceBuzz, you’re telling Google to prioritize content from a source you trust.
Retirees receiving Social Security senior benefits 
should see a benefits boost in 2027, thanks to the recently announced 
cost-of-living adjustment (COLA). On October 14, the Social Security 
Administration (SSA) announced a 3.6% COLA, the largest since 2023. The COLA 
also marks a milestone not seen since 1997, though that milestone matters less 
than it sounds. 
Here's what you should know about the COLA, its historic significance, and what 
it could mean for your benefits in 2027.

 How the COLA affects Social Security benefits
The 3.6% COLA impacts nearly 72 million Social Security beneficiaries and about 
7.3 million Supplemental Security Income (SSI) recipients. It provides a 3.6% 
boost to the benefits, adding about $75 more to the average monthly retirement 
benefit. 
According to the SSA, the COLA should bring the average retired worker's monthly 
benefit from $2,095 to $2,170 when it goes into effect in January 2027. Married 
couples should receive a combined increase of about $117 per month, raising 
their average monthly benefits to $3,355 in 2027. SSI recipients should see the 
increase beginning December 31, 2026.

 Why the COLA marks a historic milestone
The 2027 COLA marks the sixth consecutive year of COLA increases at or above 
2.5%, a streak that was last achieved from 1988 through 1997. Since the COLA 
reflects increases in inflation, this historic streak signals that consumers are 
paying higher prices. 
The 2021 and 2023 COLAs were notably large, at 5.9% and 8.7%, respectively. The 
largest COLA since 1975 was 1980's 14.3% increase. 
 The factors behind the "Trump bump"
The 2027 COLA has been called the "Trump bump," a commentator's framing tying 
the increase to the persistent 2026 inflation that's been driven, in part, by 
the war with Iran and its impact on energy prices. 
The SSA calculates the COLA based on the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage 
Earners and Clerical Workers, or CPI-W. The CPI-W tracks the average changes in 
prices that workers pay for common goods and services. The COLA calculation is 
only based on third-quarter data from July through September, so inflation that 
occurs outside of that period is not factored into the calculation.

 What the larger COLA really means
Though Social Security recipients might celebrate an increase in benefits, the 
COLA and the higher resulting benefits mean that recipients have been paying 
higher prices because of inflation. The COLA isn't intended to outpace 
inflation, but just to offset those costs, so even though benefits might 
increase, retirees aren't necessarily keeping more money in their accounts at 
the end of the month. 
Additionally, since the COLA is only calculated based on third-quarter inflation 
data, retirees are left on their own to cope with the effects of any inflation 
that occurs during the rest of the year. If inflation climbs steeply in the 
first and second quarters, retirees must pay those higher prices on their 
established benefit amounts for the year. That delay in benefits may take a 
financial toll on retirees living on fixed budgets. 
 Does the COLA accurately reflect retirees' expenses
Some experts also state that the COLA doesn't accurately reflect the expenses 
that retirees pay. The CPI-W reflects the expenses that younger workers pay, but 
it doesn't specifically track retirees' expenses. Since retirees often spend 
more of their incomes on healthcare and other expenses, the current COLA 
calculation doesn't necessarily reflect older Americans' costs. 
"Another year, another COLA that falls short of expectations," said Shannon 
Benton, Executive Director of The Senior Citizens League, in a statement. 
"Seniors will find themselves disappointed today when they look up the COLA 
announcement in the news. The reality is that millions depend on Social Security 
to retire with dignity, and today's announcement puts that ideal in jeopardy for 
millions." 
 Social Security's lost buying power
According to an analysis by The Senior Citizens League, though the COLA may be 
intended to help benefits keep up with inflation, benefits have lost significant 
buying power over time. The analysis indicates that benefits have lost 13.7% of 
their buying power over the last decade, meaning a dollar of benefits in 2016 is 
only worth $0.86 today. 
According to the analysis, benefits would need to be increased by almost $296 
per month, or about $3,550 per year, to restore their buying power for the 
average beneficiary.

 The Medicare Part B premium's impact on benefits
Medicare Part B premiums may also eat into any benefits increase brought about 
by the COLA. Medicare Part B premiums are automatically deducted from Social 
Security benefits, so if those premiums increase in 2027, those expenses might 
use up part of the benefits increase before seniors ever see the money. Official 
Medicare Part B rates haven't yet been announced for 2027. 
 Bottom line
Since the COLA is a percentage, the benefits increases that seniors should see 
in 2027 may vary. Individuals receiving lower benefits amounts should receive a 
smaller boost, while higher earners receiving larger benefits checks should see 
a larger increase. 
If you have a my Social Security account, you may use your account to enroll in 
paperless notices and see your COLA notice online, including your revised 
benefits amount, beginning in late November. If you haven't enrolled in 
paperless notices, you should receive your COLA notice by mail in December. Once 
you know your benefits amount for 2027, it may be a good idea to revisit your retirement plan and budget 
to make any adjustments necessary.
